newsitem.title: USA: Dollar/Europe gains may compel Japan to defend yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/Europe gains may compel Japan to defend yen.

text.p: Japanese officials may be forced to step up their efforts to defend the beleaguered yen if other Group of Seven nations fail to slow the dollar's current rally against European currencies, analysts said.

Japan can ill afford further yen weakness, which has exacerbated a sharp drop in Japanese stock prices, but U.S. and European leaders seem content to watch a dollar/mark rally that is pushing dollar/yen higher as well, analysts said.
"Japan has jawboned over the weak yen but there's not much it can do by itself," said Gabriele Lamers at Bank of Boston.
"There's some degree of nervousness about the dollar rising too quickly and for too long" among other G7 nations, added Lamers, an international economist at the bank.
The greenback has jumped ten pfennings, or 6.5 percent, to 1.64 marks since January 1. But dollar/yen has only risen to 119 from 116, a 2.6-percent gain, over the same period.
That represents a turnaround from the last two years, when a rising dollar/yen was generally seen pulling up dollar/mark.
After falling to post-World War II lows in early 1995, the dollar has risen 49.2 percent from 79.75 yen, but only 22 percent from 1.3438 marks.

A strong U.S. economy continues to draw investors to the dollar in general, but the popular perception that the Bank of Japan would enter the market to sell dollars near 120 yen has diverted dollar bulls to dollar/mark, analysts said.

"The Japanese are letting people know they are not encouraging a weak yen anymore and it seems to have worked, with people shifting their emphasis to the (weak) mark," added McGee, an international economist at Tokai Bank Ltd.
Some analysts doubt the BoJ would act on its own, but troubling stock market losses suggest it might, analysts said.
The Nikkei 225 .N225 has fallen 10 percent in January alone, threatening to derail Japan's nascent economic recovery.
"Japan needs to maintain confidence in its financial markets, which means the yen can't keep falling as fast as it has," McGee said.
But without the U.S. and Germany to back it up, any intervention by the BoJ might just give dip-buying dollar bulls a price break, analysts said.
"A unilateral move might just be seen as a means to get cheap dollars from the BoJ," Lamers said.

"But if you had the Bundesbank and the U.S. involved, the message would be pretty clear: they are willing to tolerate dollar/mark at 1.55 to 1.60 and dollar/yen at 115 to 120, but above that, they get a little crazy," Lamers said.
Bundesbank officials had said little during the latest dollar surge until Wednesday, when Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke spoke with reporters in Frankfurt.
Welteke said the dollar/mark rally must slow, even though the export stimulus it had brought offered "the only ray of light" for German economic growth.
Welteke also conceded that slight further depreciation of the mark would be possible.

"You've got an asymmetric position. Dollar/yen has run such a long distance," said Lars Pederson, international economist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "We're much closer to Bank of Japan intervention. I can't imagine the Germans would do anything before (dollar/mark) 1.75."

Japanese and U.S. officials stated their cases on Tuesday. Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto called the dollar's recent wild moves "scary" and Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the weak-yen trend was excessive.
But New York Federal Reserve President William McDonough chimed in with support for the longstanding strong-dollar policy of U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
Rubin later added he was not concerned the dollar's strength would worsen the U.S. trade deficit.
Mitsuzuka on Wednesday said the G7 nations support the strong dollar policy of the U.S.
G7 economic leaders will meet in Berlin on February 8, when many analysts expect a formal statement endorsing dollar strength.

U.S. officials have recently been feeling little pressure to cap the dollar, as solid economic growth with low inflation had quieted exporters who last year complained a strong dollar had damaged their international competitiveness.

On Tuesday, however, IBM said currency fluctuations had hurt fourth-quarter earnings by $0.18 per share despite nine percent revenue growth in constant currency, the best since 1985. On Wednesday morning, IBM shares tumbled more than 10 points and dragged down the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
Still, economists doubt scattered corporate complaints will weigh heavily on official U.S. policy.

"It's difficult to understand how a strong dollar is a problem with (U.S.) fourth-quarter gross domestic product up (an estimated) four percent. The U.S. will just let (Japan) do it on their own," said Pederson.
